overview.title: Training the bag-of-words model and plotting accuracy
overview.main_topic: Finishing the fit call with EarlyStopping, noting training speed, and plotting training vs. validation accuracy (figure 14.2)
overview.central_idea: The 20,001-parameter model trains in well under a minute, and tokenization and encoding cost more than the parameter updates. In figure 14.2, training accuracy keeps rising toward about 0.97 while validation accuracy levels off around 0.89 instead of falling. The authors conclude that the model is so simple it cannot really overfit.
overview.importance: This establishes the bag-of-words baseline (about 89% validation; 88% test on p.426) that bigrams, LSTMs and embeddings will be compared against. It also introduces the point that preprocessing, not model compute, can be the bottleneck for small text models, which p.426 expands on.

summary:
The page opens with the **rest of Listing 14.14**. `model.fit` receives `bag_of_words_train_ds`, `validation_data=bag_of_words_val_ds`, `epochs=10` and `callbacks=[early_stopping]`. The callback (defined on p.424) monitors `val_loss` with `patience=2` and restores the best weights.

The model **trains in much less than a minute**, which is unsurprising for 20,001 parameters. The authors point out that **tokenization and encoding of the input are actually more expensive than updating the model parameters**. Turning text into 20,000-dimensional multi-hot vectors happens on the CPU for every batch of every epoch, while the parameter update is one small matrix–vector product.

A standard matplotlib snippet then plots `history.history["accuracy"]` (red dashed) and `history.history["val_accuracy"]` (blue solid) against `epochs = range(1, len(accuracy) + 1)`, with a title and legend.

**Figure 14.2** (captioned 'Training and validation metrics for our bag of words model') shows **9 epochs**. Since `epochs=10`, early stopping ended the run one epoch early. Reading the plot approximately:

- **training accuracy** rises steadily from about 0.84 at epoch 1 to about 0.975 at epoch 9;
- **validation accuracy** starts around 0.88, reaches about 0.89 by epoch 3, and stays nearly flat (peaking near 0.893 around epoch 7).

The authors interpret this as validation performance that **levels off rather than significantly declining**: the model is so simple it cannot really overfit. The growing gap between the curves shows that the model fits the training set ever better, but the extra fit does not hurt validation accuracy much. Next, the model is evaluated on the test set (p.426, 0.88388 accuracy).

paragraphs.excerpt: Our model trains in much less than a minute, which is unsurprising given
paragraphs.what_it_says: The model trains in much less than a minute, unsurprising given its size. Tokenizing and encoding the input is actually quite a bit more expensive than updating the parameters. Next the authors plot the model accuracy (figure 14.2).
paragraphs.what_it_means: The per-batch model computation is a (32 × 20000) · (20000 × 1) product plus its gradient, which is trivial. The string processing (standardization, whitespace splitting, vocabulary lookup, building 20,000-length multi-hot rows) dominates the run time.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: For small models the input pipeline is the bottleneck. This motivates the 'Preprocessing text efficiently' sidebar on p.426 (parallel map, keeping the GPU busy, precomputing tokens).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: one batch costs about 640,000 multiply-adds forward, which is microseconds on any device. Tokenizing 32 reviews of about 230 words each (p.429 gives an average of 233) involves string operations and hash lookups that are much slower per element.

terminology.meaning: When data preparation, not model computation, limits training speed.

connections: p.426: sidebar on preprocessing text efficiently on the CPU
p.432: by contrast, the one-hot LSTM model trains very slowly

paragraphs.excerpt: We can see that validation performance levels off rather than significantly declining;
paragraphs.what_it_says: Validation performance levels off rather than significantly declining, because the model is so simple it cannot really overfit. Next, the model is evaluated on the test set.
paragraphs.what_it_means: In the usual overfitting picture, validation accuracy peaks and then falls while training accuracy keeps improving. Here it plateaus instead. The low-capacity linear model can memorize somewhat (training accuracy reaches about 97.5%), but it cannot fit noise in a way that seriously damages generalization.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: With a plateau, the exact stopping epoch hardly matters, so EarlyStopping is a convenience rather than a necessity here. Compare the LSTM on p.437, which reaches 99% training accuracy and overfits before learning good embeddings.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: 'cannot really overfit' is a strong phrasing. The train–validation gap grows to about 8 points, which is a mild form of overfitting, but the validation metric is not hurt.

concepts.name: Overfitting vs. a plateau
concepts.definition: Overfitting is when validation performance worsens as training continues, while training performance improves. A plateau is when validation stops improving but does not decline.
concepts.intuition: Studying the same practice exam over and over: eventually your score on it keeps rising, but your real-exam score stays the same (plateau) or drops (overfitting).
concepts.technical: Figure 14.2: train accuracy rises from about 0.84 to 0.975 over 9 epochs while val accuracy stays near 0.89.
concepts.significance: The authors attribute the plateau to the model's simplicity.
concepts.example: Validation accuracy in the range 0.887–0.893 from epoch 2 onward.
concepts.misconception: That any train–validation gap means harmful overfitting.

concepts.name: History object and learning curves
concepts.definition: fit() returns a History object whose .history dict holds per-epoch metric lists, which can be plotted as learning curves.
concepts.intuition: A training diary, one entry per epoch.
concepts.technical: Keys used here: "accuracy" and "val_accuracy". The x-axis is range(1, len(accuracy) + 1).
concepts.significance: It produces figure 14.2 and shows how long early stopping let training run.
concepts.misconception: That the list length always equals epochs. With EarlyStopping it can be shorter.

concepts.name: Preprocessing as the bottleneck
concepts.definition: For small models, turning raw text into tensors can take longer than the training update itself.
concepts.intuition: A chef who cooks in seconds but spends minutes chopping vegetables.
concepts.technical: TextVectorization runs inside tf.data map with num_parallel_calls=8 on the CPU, every epoch.
concepts.significance: Stated on this page, and expanded in the efficiency sidebar on p.426.
concepts.example: The whole fit takes much less than a minute, and most of it is spent on encoding.
concepts.misconception: That training speed depends only on the model's size.

code.title: Plotting training and validation accuracy
code.original_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

accuracy = history.history["accuracy"]
val_accuracy = history.history["val_accuracy"]
epochs = range(1, len(accuracy) + 1)

plt.plot(epochs, accuracy, "r--", label="Training accuracy")
plt.plot(epochs, val_accuracy, "b", label="Validation accuracy")
plt.title("Training and validation accuracy")
plt.legend()
plt.show()
code.what_it_does: Plots per-epoch training accuracy (red dashed) and validation accuracy (blue solid), producing figure 14.2.

line_explanations.explanation: Extracts the per-epoch metric lists recorded by fit().
1-based epoch numbers; the length adapts to early stopping.
"r--" = red dashed line, "b" = blue solid line; the labels feed the legend.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: history. Output: the accuracy plot.
code.theory_link: Learning curves are the main tool for diagnosing under- and overfitting (chapter 5).
pitfalls: Keys must match the metric names: "accuracy" because metrics=["accuracy"] was used in compile.
The plot shows accuracy only. To see the val_loss that EarlyStopping monitors, also plot history.history["val_loss"] (beyond the book).

plt.figure()

deeper.title: Why the run stopped at epoch 9
deeper.body: Our inference from the figure: there are 9 points, while `epochs=10`. With `patience=2`, stopping after epoch 9 means the best `val_loss` was reached at epoch 7, and epochs 8 and 9 did not improve on it. This agrees with the validation accuracy curve, which peaks around epoch 7. Because `restore_best_weights=True`, the model evaluated on p.426 has the epoch-7 weights, not the epoch-9 weights.

deeper.title: Why a linear model resists overfitting here
deeper.body: Beyond the book: 20,001 parameters against 20,000 training reviews may look like a lot, but the model can only draw a single hyperplane in word-presence space. Most vocabulary words are rare, so their weights receive few gradient updates and stay small. The frequent, sentiment-bearing words dominate. Memorizing individual reviews would require interactions between features that a linear model cannot express, so extra training mainly sharpens the confidence of existing predictions (lower training loss, higher training accuracy) without changing many validation decisions.

questions.question: According to the page, which part of training the bag-of-words model is most expensive?
options: Tokenizing and encoding the input text
questions.answer: Tokenizing and encoding the input text
questions.explanation: The authors say tokenization and encoding are quite a bit more expensive than updating the model parameters. The parameter update is tiny, validation is a forward pass of the same small model, and plotting happens after training.

questions.question: Figure 14.2 shows 9 epochs, but fit was called with epochs=10. Why?
questions.answer: The EarlyStopping callback (patience=2 on val_loss) stopped training after two epochs without improvement, so the run ended after epoch 9.
questions.explanation: The callback was passed via callbacks=[early_stopping]. Our inference is that the best val_loss was at epoch 7.

questions.question: How does figure 14.2 differ from a classic overfitting curve, and what explanation do the authors give?
questions.answer: In classic overfitting, validation accuracy peaks and then declines. Here it levels off around 0.89 while training accuracy keeps rising. The authors explain that the model is so simple it cannot really overfit.

questions.question: In the plotting code, what does the format string "r--" specify?
options: A red dotted line with markers
questions.explanation: In matplotlib, 'r' is red and '--' is dashed. It is used for training accuracy, while "b" gives a blue solid line for validation.

questions.question: If the final validation accuracy is about 0.89 on the 5,000-review validation set, roughly how many reviews are misclassified?
questions.explanation: Accuracy is the fraction correct; the validation set has 5,000 reviews (p.422).

questions.question: EarlyStopping monitors val_loss, but the figure plots accuracy. Why might these disagree about the 'best' epoch?
questions.answer: Loss measures the confidence of predictions, while accuracy only counts thresholded decisions. Val_loss can rise (overconfident wrong predictions) while val_accuracy stays flat or rises slightly, so the best epochs can differ.
questions.explanation: Beyond the book; this is why plotting val_loss as well is informative.

questions.question: Before turning the page, predict the test accuracy of this model from figure 14.2.
questions.answer: Close to the validation plateau, about 0.88–0.89. The book reports 0.88388 on p.426.
questions.explanation: Validation accuracy is a good estimate of test accuracy when the validation set has not been heavily tuned on.
